list.listitem: Key exam findings increasing the likelihood of testicular torsion include an abnormal testicular lie and an absent cremasteric reflex.C
Doppler ultrasound or scintigraphy can be used for diagnosis, provided that one of these tests is readily available and the presentation is equivocal. C
Surgical exploration of a painful scrotum should not be delayed if testicular torsion is suspected. C

background.definition: Testicular torsion is a twisting of the spermatic cord, often compromising the blood supply to the testicle and surrounding structures.

list.listitem: Annual incidence: 1 in 4000 males less than age 25.
Intravaginal torsion: congenital malformation of the processes vaginalis, allowing the testicle to rotate freely within the tunica vaginalis (90% of cases).
Trauma (4%-8% of cases).
Pubertal increase in testicular volume.
Testicular tumor.
Cryptorchidism.
Long spermatic cord.
Testicle with horizontal lie.
Venous return obstructed initially.
Equalization of venous and arterial pressures compromises arterial flow, leading to testicular ischemia.
Degree of ischemia depends on duration and degree of rotation.
Ischemia can occur in as soon as 4 hours, and is almost certain after 24 hours.
Elective orchiopexy is recommended, even if manual detorsion successful. C
Contralateral exploration and orchiopexy should also be considered. C
Scrotal pain, including posttraumatic pain that is not improving after more than one hour, is the most common presentation. C
Absence of cremasteric reflex and an abnormal testicular lie are very suspicious for testicular torsion. C
Doppler ultrasound or scintigraphy can be used for diagnosis for equivocal presentations, depending on what is most readily available. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain improvement, usually within an hour of trauma, if torsion is absent
"Blue dot sign": hard, tender, bluish nodule is often present on upper pole of testicle
Edematous "orange peel" scrotal skin, tender epididymis, pyuria, dysuria
Often diagnosed prior to any pain developing

list.listitem: The typical patient presents with the sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain.
Physical examination is unreliable so imaging or surgical intervention may be necessary if concerning symptoms.

Time is of the essence; one series reported that the testicle was saved in 90% of cases if detorsion occurred less than 6 hours from onset of symptoms, but less than 10% of cases if detorsion occurred after 24 hours.
Cremasteric reflex (elevation of testicle at least 5 mm after stroking or pinching medial thigh) is absent in most cases of torsion.
False positives for an absent cremasteric reflex can occur under age 30 months (i.e., more than half of normal boys under this age do not have this reflex).

A retrospective study of children with testicular torsion shows the most helpful signs and symptoms are: pain less than 24 hours, nausea and/or vomiting, abnormal cremasteric reflex, abdominal pain, and high position of the testes.
Although not required for diagnosis, an abnormal testicular lie is quite specific for torsion.

The TWIST score (Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Torsion) is a useful clinical tool. A "negative" score in low risk patients is adequate to rule out torsion, and a "positive" score in high risk patients can facilitate urgent surgical exploration.
Doppler ultrasound gives anatomical and real-time vascular flow information, and it is the test of choice if readily available in patients with equivocal exams.
In a study of 20 patients with acute scrotal pain, scintigraphy correctly identified all 4 patients with torsion, agreeing with prior reviews reporting sensitivity of almost 100%.
Color doppler is a reliable test for testicular torsion.
While ultrasound is the definitive test, a neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio may be helpful in the diagnosis of testicular torsion.
Surgical exploration should not be delayed if torsion is even moderately suspected.
See .
Manual detorsion may provide quick and noninvasive treatment. C
Surgical exploration should not delayed if detorsion attempt cannot be performed immediately. C
Surgical exploration and detorsion is emergent if torsion is suspected and manual detorsion is unsuccessful.
Several expert recommendations call for elective orchiopexy even if nonoperative detorsion is successful; several recommendations call for contralateral exploration and orchiopexy.
Intermittent testicular torsion may occur. Consider surgical exploration if imaging is not possible during symptomatic period.

Manual detorsion procedure: stand at the supine patient's feet and rotate the affected testicle 180 degrees away from the midline, as though opening a book. Rotation can be done with IV sedation, with or without local anesthesia.
There should be a dramatic decrease in pain if the detorsion procedure is successful. Torsion of greater than 360 degrees is possible, so more than one full rotation may be needed.
Document return of blood flow with Doppler ultrasound.
Reported success rates are 27% to 80%.
Testicle is saved in 90% of cases if detorsion occurs within 6 hours of symptom onset, but in only 10% of cases after 24 hours of symptom onset. B
Most common causes of testicular loss after torsion are delay in seeking medical attention (58%), incorrect diagnosis (29%), and delay in treatment (13%).B
Even if orchiopexy is performed in the situations noted above, recurrent torsion has been documented at a 4% to 5% rate.B
Seek medical attention immediately for scrotal pain.
The torsed testicle can almost always be saved if surgery happens within 6 hours of symptoms.
The torsed testicle is almost always lost if surgery happens after 24 hours of symptoms.

In one series, 65% of children under 2 years old with painful scrotums had testicular torsion; this percentage decreased dramatically for age 18 or older (92% in this age group had epididymitis, not torsion).
